Let me walk you through what we're seeing on NCDC1 at your Livingston facility — and it's a field that's telling a very clear story once you know what to look at. Looking at the full month of May, the load traces are elevated above the 586 kVA daily supply target for roughly 85 to 90 percent of available hours. This machine is working hard, continuously. The challenge is that it's doing that work inefficiently. The average power factor is 85.0% — which means for every dollar of electricity the utility is pushing through that transformer, about 15 cents is circulating as reactive energy. It's not producing anything useful. It's generating heat, stressing the windings, and loading your supply circuit with invisible burden. At its worst moments in the month, that power factor dropped to 70.0%. At 70%, nearly a third of your electricity is wasted. The numbers that come out of that inefficiency are concrete. It is pure electromagnetic overhead — and it is costing you approximately $209,767 per year in measurable energy losses. Now layer in the thermal consequence. A transformer generating reactive losses generates heat. At 267.9 kVAR average reactive circulation, the thermal burden on NCDC1 is approximately 277,515 BTU per hour. That heat has to go somewhere — and it goes into the transformer windings, into the electrical room, and into the cooling system. Your cooling infrastructure is drawing 40.5 kilowatts of electricity at a cost of roughly $7.96 per hour to fight that heat. You are paying twice: once to generate the reactive heat, and again to remove it. MPTS correction eliminates the reactive source — which means the cooling system works less, lasts longer, and costs less to operate. The harmonic layer adds a third dimension of stress. At 6.0% continuous and 10.7% peak, you're running above that threshold every day. They also create voltage waveform distortion that stresses variable frequency drives and sensitive controls downstream. The voltage stability picture confirms the load character of this facility. The voltage field on NCDC1 is not failing — but it is under pressure, and the V view makes that pressure visible in detail. The measured average voltage is 481.5 volts, sitting just marginally above the 480V line-to-line nominal. At first glance, that sounds acceptable. But the story is in the shape of the trace, not just the average.

The voltage band across the month spans from a ceiling near 500 volts down to a floor near 460 volts. That 40-volt spread tells you this field is not a stable, well-regulated supply. It is a reactive-burdened field breathing in and out with load cycling, and the triangular voltage-drop signatures visible throughout the trace confirm that inductive load cycling — compressors, conveyors, motor starts — is the dominant driver.

Those triangular drops are not isolated events. They cluster most densely in the 260502 through 260515 window, appearing with enough regularity and consistency to tell you that whatever equipment is driving them is operating on a repeating duty cycle throughout the production shift. And when voltage dips 10 to 20 volts below the 480V nominal — even briefly — that is enough to stress motor windings, cause variable frequency drives to compensate or fault, and push contactors toward dropout threshold.

The two significant disturbance events are worth calling out directly. The event near 260508 is the more severe — the blue voltage trace drops sharply and dramatically, well below the nominal line, consistent with either a supply interruption or a major load switching event. The event near 260523 is less severe but still visible as a distinct voltage disruption.

For a food processing facility of this scale, with refrigeration compressors and processing equipment on continuous duty, repeated under-voltage excursions accelerate insulation aging in motor windings, reduce variable frequency drive headroom, and increase the probability of nuisance trips during peak load intervals. The device-health risk here is rated moderate-to-high based on voltage pattern alone — before harmonics are even factored in.

Start with the reactive layer. The kVAR average from the BT header is 267.9 kVAR, and the kVAR MAX is 445.5 kVAR. That maximum figure is the critical number for sizing — it represents the peak reactive demand this transformer must absorb at any given operational moment. Every kVAR circulating in that field is doing no useful work. It is heat, it is current, and it is transformer stress. At 267.9 kVAR average, roughly 30 to 35 percent of the apparent power flowing through this transformer is reactive burden, not productive output.

The amperage picture reinforces this. The M-view red amperage trace runs dense and elevated throughout the month, with a recorded maximum of 701.2 amps. On a 2,500 kVA transformer at 480 volts, the nameplate current ceiling is approximately 3,005 amps three-phase — so 701.2 amps is well within nameplate limits in aggregate. But the sustained density of that amperage trace, combined with the reactive component, means the transformer is carrying significant I-squared-R losses continuously. At peak moments of 10.7%, the harmonic stress nearly doubles. Those harmonics generate additional eddy-current heating in the transformer core and create interference that degrades power quality across downstream connected equipment.

The combination — 85.0% power factor, 445.5 kVAR peak reactive demand, and 6.0% harmonic content — is a compounding stress signature. Each element makes the others worse. MPTS correction addresses the reactive layer directly and reduces the current amplitude that feeds the harmonic-driven heating cycle.

**Reactive Compensation Priority:** The 445.5 kVAR MAX reading establishes a clear sizing requirement. Two H490 units provide sufficient reactive correction headroom with reserve capacity. This should be the primary engineering action item.

An engineering review of the largest motor loads on this transformer, particularly refrigeration compressors, is recommended to assess insulation condition and VFD parameter tuning. **Outage Root Cause Investigation:** Two unplanned interruptions in a single month — particularly the May 8th event estimated at 60 to 90 minutes — warrant review of the upstream supply and switching gear serving this transformer. For a continuous food processing and cold storage operation, supply reliability is a food safety and product integrity issue, not only an energy issue.

**Thermal Monitoring:** Given the 277,515 BTU per hour thermal burden, infrared thermography of the transformer and associated switchgear is recommended on a quarterly basis until MPTS correction is commissioned.
